title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
oneLiner: Before answering, let the AI look up the right pages from your own documents (or a knowledge graph) and answer from them: an open-book exam instead of a closed-book one.

what.html:
RAG = retrieve, augment, generate. When a question comes in, the system searches your documents for the few most relevant passages, adds them to the prompt, and the language model answers from them. Most of the craft is arithmetic: how many passages fit, how to cut documents into pieces, how to measure whether the right pieces were found, and how fast it all runs.

Everyday versionA brilliant scholar who has been locked in a room for a year doesn't know today's news or your company's rules. Hand them the right files before they answer.

why.html:
• Answers can use current, private information without retraining the model.
  • Answers can cite sources, and hallucination drops.
  • Almost every real AI assistant over company documents works this way.

how.title: What LLMs can't do alone
how.html: Out-of-date knowledge, no private data, made-up answers, forgetting long chats. Retraining for every change is far too slow and costly.

how.title: The open-book flow
how.html: "Can I sit the exam with 70% attendance?" → find the attendance-policy paragraphs (not the hostel rules) → paste them into the prompt → answer from them.

how.title: How many passages to keep
how.html: Keep the best K, or everything above a quality bar. Too many floods the model with noise; too few leaves out the answer. A second, smarter re-ranking pass helps when scores are nearly tied.

how.title: The space in the prompt
how.html: 8,192 total − 300 for instructions − 220 for the question leaves 7,672, room for 14 passages of 512 tokens. Long chats eat this space turn by turn.

how.title: Cutting documents into pieces
how.html: Overlap neighbouring pieces so ideas at the edges aren't cut in half. A step of 600 − 120 = 480 tokens turns an 18,200-token document into 38 pieces.

how.title: Did we fetch the right pieces?
how.html: Precision: how much of what was fetched was useful (2 of 5 = 0.4). Recall: how much of the useful material was fetched (2 of 2 = 1.0).

how.title: Fast enough?
how.html: Add up each step's time: with 2,500 ms allowed and 2,170 ms used, a 300 ms re-ranker fits but a 400 ms one doesn't.

how.title: When to walk a graph
how.html: "Which course is Rahul in?" is a simple lookup. "How are Rahul and Dr. Vidhi related?" needs a path through a knowledge graph: Rahul → NLP ← Dr. Vidhi.

how.title: Graphs and language models together
how.html: Graphs give checked facts and paths (if a data centre fails, which customers are hit?); language models read text and can even build the graphs.

how.title: Beyond text, beyond one search
how.html: Search charts and photos too, and let an agent plan, search, check what's missing and search again (nuclear vs solar output) before answering with sources.

demo.html: See how a question whose answer lives in a chart or a photo is handled: with a model that understands images, or by first describing every image and table in words.

example.html:
Counting pieces. Chunks of 600 tokens overlapping by 120 advance 480 tokens each time. 18,200 ÷ 480 = 37.9, rounded up to 38 because the leftover end still becomes a short piece. By contrast, "how many 512-token pieces fit in 7,672 tokens?" rounds down to 14, because you can't exceed the limit.

Supplementary Retrieved documents can contain hidden instructions ("ignore previous rules…"); good systems treat retrieved text strictly as information, never as commands.

misunderstandings: It only changes the prompt at question time.
More retrieved text is always better.
Noise and budget limits hurt answers.
Top-K and thresholding are the same.
Only when relationships are the answer.
takeaways: Stride = size − overlap; ⌈doc/stride⌉ chunks; precision/recall vs a golden set.
Latency adds up; graphs for multi-hop; multimodal and agentic loops.
thirty: LLMs have cut-offs, no private knowledge, hallucinate and degrade in long chats; retraining is too heavy. RAG retrieves relevant chunks by semantic search, augments the prompt and generates a grounded answer (attendance policy example). Selection: top-K (fixed count) vs threshold (quality bar, e.g. 0.80); too many = noise and budget burn, too few = missing info; re-rank near-tied scores. Token budget: Available = Max − (System + Query): 10,000 − 500 = 9,500; 8,192 − 520 = 7,672 → ⌊7,672/512⌋ = 14 chunks; compaction past ~80%. Chunking: stride = size − overlap; 18,200 tokens, 600/120 → stride 480 → ⌈37.9⌉ = 38. Retrieval precision/recall vs a golden set: 2 of 5 → P 0.4, R 1.0; 10 of 1000 → P 0.01; 13 of 20 → R 0.65. Latency = embed + retrieve + re-rank + generate: 2,500 − 2,170 = 330 ms → 300 ms re-ranker fits. Graph RAG for relationship/multi-hop questions (Rahul → NLP ← Dr. Vidhi; blast radius); vectors for textual similarity; KG–LLM synergy. Multimodal RAG embeds images/tables or narrates them; agentic RAG loops plan → retrieve → reason, needing evaluation of each step.
